 Storms Hail the size of golf balls pummels parts of Arizona as rare storm moves through the West
 Tornado watches were issued for multiple areas — the first the state has seen since October 2010. Listen to this article with a free profile 00:00 00:00 
 Powerful storms bring heavy winds and rain to Arizona 01:41 Get more news Live on Share Add NBC News to Google Oct. 22, 2026, 6:51 AM EDT  /  Updated   Oct. 22, 2026, 6:51 AM EDT / Source : The Associated Press By The Associated Press PHOENIX — Hail the size of golf balls and damaging wind gusts pounded northern and central Arizona in a rare storm blowing through, bringing with it tornado risks and possible flash floods. 
 The National Weather Service issued multiple warnings as severe thunderstorms moved through the state overnight Tuesday and into Wednesday, encouraging people to seek shelter and stay away from windows as damaging 2- to 3-inch) hail struck the area. Hail pummeled roofs, shattered windows and dented cars. 
 A lightning strike in Chandler, Ariz., on Tuesday. Gwendelyn Irey via AP Tornado watches were issued for multiple areas — the first the state has seen since October 2010.

 Slide 1 of 1 Warm, moist air moving north fuels storms coming off the California coast. Changing winds can make them spin, creating the conditions for tornadoes, said Ryan Bernhart, a weather service meteorologist in Flagstaff.
 Golf ball-sized hail and powerful wind gusts battered northern and central Arizona, damaging homes and vehicles. Armando Penaloza via AP “This is very unusual for this area at this time of the year,” Bernhart said.
 Strong winds toppled trees in Flagstaff and Mesa, with some landing on walls and carports. A few dozen ponderosa pines over 30 feet tall fell down in the Coconino National Forest, northwest of Flagstaff. 
 “These are not small trees that are down," Bernhart said. “These are pretty strong trees that had been knocked down.”
 The greatest threat to the Phoenix metro area is heavy rainfall and flash flooding tonight and Thursday morning, said Mark O’Malley, a meteorologist at the weather service office in Phoenix.
